content.thinking:
The user is asking from a product trio perspective (Product Manager, Designer, Engineer) - what gaps or blind spots exist in their current analysis that they haven't yet discovered or explored. This is a strategic/product thinking question, not a data analysis task. I should respond with text only since this is a synthesis/thinking question.

Let me think through what a product trio (PM, Designer, Tech Lead/Engineer) would care about that hasn't been covered:

**From the PM lens:**
- Success metrics - what does "OTEP ingestion working well" look like? No KPIs defined
- User journey - who are the applicants? What's their experience if they see only 160 gigs?
- Agency admin experience - the remediation report is a file they receive, but is there a better workflow?
- Prioritization - which agencies to fix first for maximum impact? (EnterpriseGov unlocks 178 in one go)
- Launch readiness criteria - what's the minimum viable gig count for launch?
- Ongoing operations - who owns ingestion after launch? Is this a one-time or recurring process?
- Feedback loop - how do agencies know their gig was blocked?

**From the Designer lens:**
- The applicant experience with only 160 gigs and many stale listings
- The remediation report is an Excel file - is that the right UX for agencies to understand what happened and fix it?
- How blocked gigs appear to applicants - do they see nothing, or an error state?
- Empty state design - if an applicant filters by Function and gets 0 results, what do they see?
- Duplicate gig problem - same opportunity posted multiple times with different tags?

**From the Engineer/Tech lens:**
- The ingestion pipeline lacks retry and re-run mechanisms, and it's unclear whether it does full replacement or delta sync
- How updates propagate when an agency fixes a gig after ingestion, and whether staleness is checked at ingestion time or on the listing page
- Test entries in production need permanent exclusion, there's no audit trail for blocked gigs, and the manual remediation report could be automated as a pre-flight check

**Strategic/Product blind spots:**
I'm noticing several gaps around duplicate gigs appearing under different tags, agencies having no visibility into blocks until the report arrives, and the minimum viable catalogue size needed for credibility at launch. The re-ingestion cadence matters too - if agencies fix gigs today, when do they actually show up? With only 160 gigs, filtering by type or function could leave applicants seeing nearly empty results, which hurts trust. There's also the issue of seven gigs with no named owner and whether those GigOwners are still in their roles, plus the risk of duplicate test entries polluting the live data.

**Operational/Technical unknowns:**
I'm also tracking whether updates to gigs already on OTEP get reflected when agencies change fields in the source system, whether applicant counts carry over or reset, and if secondment gigs - the most common type - are reaching the right audience. Some secondments might be internal to a single agency rather than truly cross-government, which raises the question of whether they belong on a whole-of-government platform. There's no clear SLA for how long agencies have to remediate blocked gigs before the next ingestion, and I'm seeing 27 blocked gigs with no LocationName that may have deeper data quality issues.

**Product trio perspectives:**
Now I'm thinking about what a product manager would prioritize - success metrics like gig fill rate and time-to-fill, whether 160 gigs is a viable launch catalogue, who owns data quality long-term, and what happens to applicant data from the old system. A designer would want to understand if anyone's actually talked to applicants about their needs, how the experience feels when browsing categories with very few gigs, and whether the remediation report assumes agencies have capable admins who can actually act on it.

From an engineering angle, there are critical questions about how ingestion actually works - whether it's incremental or full reload, what triggers a run, how deletions propagate, and whether those three test entries can be automatically filtered out rather than manually managed. There's also the question of what SLA we're targeting for a gig to appear after being fixed in the source system.

The bigger picture gaps are becoming clearer: there's no defined success metric for what "good" ingestion looks like, agencies have no real-time visibility into why their gigs are blocked, the sync cadence and triggers are undefined, and we haven't even analyzed whether duplicate gigs are a problem.

Beyond the data quality issues, there are product and operational concerns I'm realizing - applicants won't carry over from the old system so we might lose engagement, some secondments are internal transfers that shouldn't be visible government-wide, there's no clear remediation workflow for agencies to signal they're ready for re-ingestion, and we don't even know who has write access to fix those 27 blank-agency entries. We also haven't discussed whether 160 gigs is a viable launch threshold, or whether we could add pre-publish validation to catch issues before they hit the catalogue.

I'm thinking about how to frame this through a product trio lens.

content.text:
Good framing — a product trio would push beyond data quality into the full opportunity lifecycle. Here's what the current analysis hasn't touched:

**Product Manager gaps**

The analysis identifies what's broken but never defines what "good" looks like. There are no success metrics — no target fill rate, no minimum viable gig count for a credible launch, no application rate baseline. Launching OTEP with 160 gigs (25% of open opportunities) may technically work but could be perceived as a thin catalogue. The question of "what's the threshold before we go live?" hasn't been asked.

There's also no feedback loop defined. Agencies currently have no real-time signal that their gig was blocked — they'll only know when the remediation report lands in their inbox. A PM would ask: should the platform notify gig owners immediately when their gig fails validation, rather than batch-reporting it?

Post-launch operations are entirely undefined. Who owns data quality on an ongoing basis? What's the SLA for an agency to fix a blocked gig? What triggers a re-ingestion run — is it scheduled, manual, or event-driven? If an agency fixes their gig today, when does it appear on OTEP?

**Designer gaps**

No one has talked to applicants. The entire analysis is supply-side (agency data quality). The demand-side question — what do public officers actually want from an opportunity marketplace — is unasked. A designer would want to know: do applicants filter by Function? If yes, the 174 gigs missing Function become a discoverability problem beyond just ingestion.

The remediation report is an Excel file delivered to agency admins. That's a distribution mechanism, not a product experience. A designer would ask whether the admin workflow should be a self-service portal where agencies can see their blocked gigs, fix them inline, and trigger re-validation — rather than a file they receive and return manually.

The empty-state experience also hasn't been designed. STIP has only 7 open gigs. SJR has 39. If an applicant filters by type or function and gets near-zero results, what do they see? "No results found" with 160 total gigs is a trust problem on day one.

**Engineer gaps**

The ingestion logic handles the initial load but says nothing about the steady state. How are updates handled — if an agency edits a gig that's already live on OTEP, does it update in place or require a full re-ingest? How are deletions handled — if an agency closes a gig in the source, does it disappear from OTEP automatically or linger?

Duplicate gig detection hasn't been done. The same opportunity may have been posted multiple times under different tags or by different owners. No deduplication logic exists in the current design.

The 3 test entries (`Testing 2`, `[Test] Gig`, `[STIP] Test form collection`) are in the source data with Open status. Manually excluding them each run isn't sustainable — there's no permanent exclusion mechanism and no sandbox environment. A new test entry created tomorrow would reappear in the next ingestion.

The 27 gigs with no LocationName (blank agency) have no named owner and no mechanism for anyone to claim or fix them centrally. Someone with admin write access to the source system needs to handle these — that person and their access level hasn't been identified.

**The one gap across all three**

Nobody has asked whether the source data model is the right one for OTEP at all. The current design forces OTEP to derive opportunity type from a free-text name prefix — a fragile workaround for the absence of a Type field in the source. A proper fix is a structured Type column in the creation form, not a regex on GigName. Since the creation form can't be touched now, this is the technical debt that will accumulate with every new non-standard tag agencies invent. At some point the trio needs to agree on a timeline to fix it at source, not just manage it at the pipeline layer.

input.content:
Project OTEP — OTG Platform Ingestion Date 9 June 2026 Type Product trio working session prep Status Draft for discussion

How do we get OTEP to launch with a catalogue people can actually use?

A working session to align on the problems we're actually solving, ideate on solutions, and make the decisions we've been deferring.

Before we start
We've completed a full ingestion analysis. The headline: 473 of 633 open gigs (75%) will not ingest today. This isn't just a data quality problem — it surfaces three harder questions about our product, our process, and our relationship with agencies. This session is about those questions.

Context — what we know

The ingestion pipeline reads from the OTG source file and imports opportunities into OTEP. A gig is blocked if any of 7 required fields is missing or its type tag is unrecognised. We cannot modify the creation form at source. The remediation path today is: analysis → Excel report → distribute to agencies → agencies fix → re-ingest.

The numbers that should concern us most aren't the 473 blocked gigs. They're:

  • 160 — the number of gigs that would appear on OTEP at launch. Is that enough?
  • 346 — open gigs with a past end date. Ingesting these makes OTEP look abandoned.
  • 0 — number of agency admins who currently know their gig was blocked.
  • ∞ — how many new gigs will arrive with the same problems after launch, with no gate to stop them.

Design principles for this session

Agree on these before ideating. They'll help us reject ideas that feel good but don't hold up.

1
Agencies are partners, not a compliance problem

The remediation report treats data quality as an agency failure. Better framing: we haven't given agencies the tools to succeed. Solutions should reduce friction for them, not add governance overhead.

2
2
A thin catalogue at launch is worse than a delayed launch

160 gigs across all of government will feel empty, especially after filtering. If users search for Gig opportunities in a specific function and get 3 results, they'll conclude OTEP isn't for them. We should define a minimum viable catalogue before setting a go-live date.

3
Fix the recurring problem, not just the current instance

Even if agencies fix all 473 gigs today, the next batch of gigs posted without a [prefix] will hit the same wall. Solutions should have a "prevention" layer, not just a "remediation" layer.

4
The ingestion logic is temporary scaffolding

Deriving type from a free-text name prefix via regex is a workaround, not a data model. Every solution we build on top of it inherits its fragility. We should be planning to replace it, not extending it.

Problem areas — trio perspectives + ideas

Five problem areas surfaced from the analysis. For each: how PM, Designer, and Engineer see it differently — then our "how might we" and candidate solutions.

Problem area 1 of 5
Agencies have no feedback loop — they don't know their gigs are blocked
0 agencies currently notified
Product Manager

This is a trust problem. If an agency posts a gig, waits two weeks, and it never appears — they'll stop using OTG. We need to close the loop within hours, not weeks. Who owns communicating this? Is it the ingestion pipeline, the platform team, or OTG?

Designer

An Excel report is not a feedback loop — it's a post-mortem. The right moment to surface a problem is when the gig is created, not weeks later. Even if we can't touch the creation form, could we surface validation in a pre-submission preview or a gig management dashboard?

Engineer

The ingestion pipeline already knows why each gig was blocked — we're just not doing anything with that output. We could write failures to a database and serve them via a simple API. The engineering effort to notify is lower than the effort to build the analysis we just did.

"How might we surface ingestion failures to agency admins before they even ask?"
Quick win (days) Medium (weeks) Big bet (months)
Automated email per gig owner on ingestion failure Quick
Ingestion pipeline emails GigOwner directly with the specific field(s) missing. No new UI needed. Works within existing email infrastructure. Risk: email fatigue if agencies have many blocked gigs.
Agency admin dashboard — "Your gigs on OTEP" Medium
A read-only web view per agency showing all their gigs: which are live, which are blocked (and why), which are stale. No write access needed — just visibility. Would reduce the need for the remediation Excel entirely.
Batch remediation digest — weekly per agency Medium
Instead of an ad-hoc Excel file, generate a styled HTML email digest every Monday showing each agency their current blocked gigs. Owned by the pipeline, not the platform team. Scales automatically.
Inline validation in OTG at point of gig creation Big bet
Requires touching the source creation form — currently out of scope. Worth flagging as the right long-term fix. Would prevent the problem entirely rather than detect it post-hoc. Track as future work with OTG product owner.
Problem area 2 of 5
The type classification system is too fragile to maintain
163 gigs unclassifiable today · grows with every new tag variant
Product Manager

Every time an agency invents a new tag like [OCMO 2026] or [Innofest], we have to update the regex and re-run classification. That's not a product — that's ongoing maintenance. We need to own the taxonomy, not react to it.

Designer

The [prefix] convention was never designed — it emerged organically. Agencies are using it to communicate programme context ([KidSTART], [agilePSD-LDS]), not opportunity type. We're asking one field to do two different jobs. Those should be separate.

Engineer

The regex approach has a ceiling. We have 21 unrecognised tag variants today. In 12 months we'll have 50. The right model is a controlled lookup table — a list of approved tags mapped to canonical types — maintained by a product owner, not hardcoded in a script.

"How might we own the tag taxonomy rather than react to whatever agencies create?"
Publish a canonical tag list and communicate it to agencies Quick
A one-page reference doc: approved [prefix] tags, what type they map to, what each type means. Circulate to all agency admins. Doesn't fix existing gigs but prevents new variants from being invented.
Tag lookup table in the ingestion pipeline — admin-editable Medium
Replace the regex with a database table: tag_pattern → canonical_type. A non-engineer can add "[KidSTART] = Secondment" without a code deploy. Unknown tags are surfaced for classification rather than silently TBC'd.
Classify unrecognised tags with a short BO review workflow Medium
New unknown tags are queued for the BO to classify once. Once classified, all gigs with that tag are retroactively updated. Prevents the 109-gig TBC problem from recurring.
Structured Type field in OTG creation form Big bet
The permanent fix. A dropdown with approved types means no free-text prefix parsing needed. Requires OTG product owner buy-in and form change. Could be phased: add the field as optional first, then make mandatory.
Problem area 3 of 5
346 stale gigs will pollute the catalogue if ingested
55% of open gigs have a past end date · 255 have zero applicants
Product Manager

Stale listings destroy applicant trust faster than an empty catalogue. One "Application closed 14 months ago" listing and the user questions everything. We need a clear policy before go-live: do we ingest stale gigs, flag them, or exclude them?

Designer

There are two types of "stale": accidentally stale (agency forgot to close it) and intentionally open-ended (standing roles with no fixed end date). These need different UX treatments. An evergreen posting shouldn't require a fake end date just to pass validation.

Engineer

Staleness is easy to compute — GigEnd < today AND Status = Open. The harder question is what the pipeline does with the result. Exclude entirely: simple. Flag for applicant visibility: requires a OTEP listing-page change. Auto-close: requires a write-back to OTG. Three very different engineering scopes.

"How might we protect the applicant experience from stale listings without penalising agencies that use rolling end dates?"
Hard exclude stale gigs from ingestion (GigEnd < today) Quick
Simplest pipeline rule. Pros: clean catalogue, no stale listings. Cons: excludes legitimate evergreen roles. Mitigate by adding a "Evergreen / No fixed end date" checkbox to the creation form — but that requires a form change.
Auto-exclude stale + zero-applicant gigs only Quick
More permissive: only exclude gigs that are both past their end date AND have never received a single application. 255 gigs would be excluded. Gigs with at least one applicant stay in, on the assumption someone intentionally kept them open.
Surface "Closing soon" / "Recently closed" state on listing card Medium
Ingest stale gigs but show a visual indicator ("Applications may have closed") on the OTEP card. Lets applicants self-select. Requires a listing page UI change. Puts the decision with the applicant, not the pipeline.
Automated stale gig notification to agency admin Medium
30 days before expiry: "Your gig [X] closes in 30 days — extend or close it in OTG." Prevents the backlog from growing. Requires knowing who the admin is (GigOwner) and a reliable email channel.
Problem area 4 of 5
160 gigs may not be enough to launch with
No minimum viable catalogue threshold defined
Product Manager

We've never defined what "enough" looks like. 160 total gigs is already thin. After filtering by agency, type, or function, some views will return single digits. We need to decide: is there a minimum count before we go live, and if so, who unblocks it?

Designer

The problem isn't just count — it's distribution. Even 400 gigs is fine if they're spread across types and functions. But 160 gigs that are 70% Secondments from two agencies means most filter combinations return nothing. We should model what the filtered experience looks like, not just the total.

Engineer

We can model the catalogue at any threshold. If we know which agencies are willing to remediate, we can estimate the realistic passing count post-cleanup. The engineering question is how frequently we can re-run ingestion — if it's daily, agencies can fix and see results quickly.

"How might we define 'good enough to launch' before we pick a go-live date?"
Define minimum viable catalogue: count × distribution Quick
Decision, not engineering. Propose a threshold — e.g. 300 passing gigs, at least 3 opportunity types with 20+ gigs each. Get BO and leadership sign-off before committing to a go-live date.
Target-agency remediation blitz before launch Quick
Enterprise Singapore alone = 178 blocked gigs. A single focused session with their admin team unlocks 38% of all blocked content. Prioritise the top 3 agencies (EnterpriseGov, MTI, MSF) for white-glove remediation support before go-live.
Model catalogue distribution at each remediation milestone Medium
Run a simulation: what does OTEP look like if only EnterpriseGov fixes their gigs? What if MTI also fixes? Build a heat-map of gig coverage by type × function so designers can validate the browse experience at each milestone.
Problem area 5 of 5
Ingestion is a one-time event in our heads, but a recurring operation in practice
Sync cadence, update handling, and ownership undefined
Product Manager

We've been talking about "the ingestion" as if it happens once. But gigs are created, edited, closed, and re-opened continuously. Who runs the ingestion after launch — and how often? If an agency fixes a gig on Tuesday, when does it appear on OTEP? If the answer is "next month", we have a product gap.

Designer

From an applicant's perspective: if I apply for a gig on Monday and it closes on Wednesday, am I notified? If an agency edits the role description after ingestion, does OTEP reflect it? These are continuity-of-experience questions that the current pipeline design doesn't answer.

Engineer

There are three models: (1) full re-ingest on a schedule — simple but slow; (2) delta sync based on DateModified — efficient but requires reliable timestamps; (3) event-driven on OTG save — real-time but requires OTG to emit events. The choice affects how quickly fixes appear on OTEP.

"How might we make OTEP feel live — not like a monthly snapshot?"
Daily scheduled full re-ingest Quick
Run the full pipeline every night. Gigs fixed by an agency appear on OTEP within 24 hours. Simple to operate; no need to track which gigs changed. Acceptable latency for most use cases. Start here.
Delta sync on DateModified — near real-time updates Medium
On each run, only process gigs where DateModified > last_run_timestamp. Reduces processing load. Requires DateModified to be reliably updated in OTG (verify this assumption — some edits may not touch it).
Define and communicate the sync SLA to agencies Quick
Whatever cadence we choose, tell agencies explicitly: "Fixes made before 6pm will appear on OTEP by 9am the next morning." Sets expectations and gives agencies confidence the system is working.

Decisions we need to make this session

These are the blockers. Until they're resolved, the engineering team is building on assumptions.

Decision Owner Deadline Stakes if deferred
What is the minimum viable catalogue for launch? (count + distribution) BO + PM This session No go-live date can be set without it
Is time commitment required for agilePSD and Other (TBC) types? BO This session 109 gigs stuck in amber; remediation report is incomplete
How do we handle stale gigs? (exclude / flag / warn) Trio This session 346 gigs need a disposition; pipeline cannot be finalised without this rule
What is the ingestion cadence? (daily / delta / event-driven) Eng lead This session Determines how quickly agency fixes appear on OTEP; affects agency comms
Who owns the tag taxonomy going forward? PM This session Without an owner, new unclassifiable tags will accumulate after launch
What is the agency feedback mechanism? (email / dashboard / digest) Trio Next sprint Without this, blocked gigs will silently accumulate post-launch
Is there a plan to add a structured Type field in OTG? (timeline + owner) PM Next quarter Without it, type classification remains a regex workaround indefinitely

Proposed session agenda — 90 minutes

0:00 – 0:10
Context alignment discuss Walk through the 5 headline numbers. Agree we're solving the recurring problem, not just the current instance.
0:10 – 0:25
Minimum viable catalogue decide What does OTEP need to look like at launch? Define a threshold. Set the go-live gate.
0:25 – 0:40
Stale gig policy + ingestion cadence decide Choose a staleness rule. Choose a sync cadence. Both are needed before pipeline finalisation.
0:40 – 1:00
Agency feedback loop ideation ideate Pick the highest-value, lowest-effort feedback mechanism for launch. Dot vote on the 4 options in Problem Area 1.
1:00 – 1:15
Tag taxonomy + type classification decide Confirm BO ruling on agilePSD TC rule. Assign taxonomy owner. Agree on lookup table approach vs regex.
1:15 – 1:30
Parking lot + next steps discuss Capture deferred items. Assign actions. Set follow-up cadence (recommend fortnightly trio check-in on OTEP ingestion health).

North star for the quarter

What good looks like
By end of Q3: OTEP launches with a catalogue of at least 350 passing gigs across a minimum of 4 opportunity types. Agency admins receive automated feedback within 24 hours of a gig failing ingestion. The ingestion pipeline runs daily. The tag taxonomy is owned by a named person and documented in a canonical reference. Stale gigs are automatically excluded from the catalogue. The plan to move to a structured Type field in OTG is on the roadmap.
The longer game
The ingestion pipeline is temporary. The permanent solution is a reliable data model in OTG — a Type dropdown, mandatory fields enforced at save, and a real-time event stream to OTEP. Every decision we make in this session should be reversible when that day comes. Build the pipeline in a way that can be deprecated cleanly.

Pre-read for attendees

  • 01_summary_dashboard.html — overall ingestion health; read this first
  • 02_agency_breakdown.html — blocked gigs by agency and type; useful context for the remediation blitz discussion
  • 03_unrecognised_type_analysis.html — the 163 unclassifiable gigs; context for the tag taxonomy decision
  • 04_oqa_risks_assumptions.html — open questions, risks, and assumptions; the full decision log
  • OTEP_Remediation_Report_v2.xlsx — the per-agency remediation report; share with agency admins after the session
OTEP Product Trio Working Session Prep  ·  9 June 2026  ·  Draft — circulate 48 hours before the session

Agree on these before ideating. They'll help us reject ideas that feel good but don't hold up.

1
Agencies are partners, not a compliance problem

The remediation report treats data quality as an agency failure. Better framing: we haven't given agencies the tools to succeed. Solutions should reduce friction for them, not add governance overhead.

2
2
A thin catalogue at launch is worse than a delayed launch

160 gigs across all of government will feel empty, especially after filtering. If users search for Gig opportunities in a specific function and get 3 results, they'll conclude OTEP isn't for them. We should define a minimum viable catalogue before setting a go-live date.

3
Fix the recurring problem, not just the current instance

Even if agencies fix all 473 gigs today, the next batch of gigs posted without a [prefix] will hit the same wall. Solutions should have a "prevention" layer, not just a "remediation" layer.

4
The ingestion logic is temporary scaffolding

Deriving type from a free-text name prefix via regex is a workaround, not a data model. Every solution we build on top of it inherits its fragility. We should be planning to replace it, not extending it.

Problem areas — trio perspectives + ideas

Five problem areas surfaced from the analysis. For each: how PM, Designer, and Engineer see it differently — then our "how might we" and candidate solutions.

Problem area 1 of 5
Agencies have no feedback loop — they don't know their gigs are blocked
0 agencies currently notified
Product Manager

This is a trust problem. If an agency posts a gig, waits two weeks, and it never appears — they'll stop using OTG. We need to close the loop within hours, not weeks. Who owns communicating this? Is it the ingestion pipeline, the platform team, or OTG?

Designer

An Excel report is not a feedback loop — it's a post-mortem. The right moment to surface a problem is when the gig is created, not weeks later. Even if we can't touch the creation form, could we surface validation in a pre-submission preview or a gig management dashboard?

Engineer

The ingestion pipeline already knows why each gig was blocked — we're just not doing anything with that output. We could write failures to a database and serve them via a simple API. The engineering effort to notify is lower than the effort to build the analysis we just did.

"How might we surface ingestion failures to agency admins before they even ask?"
Quick win (days) Medium (weeks) Big bet (months)
Automated email per gig owner on ingestion failure Quick
Ingestion pipeline emails GigOwner directly with the specific field(s) missing. No new UI needed. Works within existing email infrastructure. Risk: email fatigue if agencies have many blocked gigs.
Agency admin dashboard — "Your gigs on OTEP" Medium
A read-only web view per agency showing all their gigs: which are live, which are blocked (and why), which are stale. No write access needed — just visibility. Would reduce the need for the remediation Excel entirely.
Batch remediation digest — weekly per agency Medium
Instead of an ad-hoc Excel file, generate a styled HTML email digest every Monday showing each agency their current blocked gigs. Owned by the pipeline, not the platform team. Scales automatically.
Inline validation in OTG at point of gig creation Big bet
Requires touching the source creation form — currently out of scope. Worth flagging as the right long-term fix. Would prevent the problem entirely rather than detect it post-hoc. Track as future work with OTG product owner.
Problem area 2 of 5
The type classification system is too fragile to maintain
163 gigs unclassifiable today · grows with every new tag variant
Product Manager

Every time an agency invents a new tag like [OCMO 2026] or [Innofest], we have to update the regex and re-run classification. That's not a product — that's ongoing maintenance. We need to own the taxonomy, not react to it.

Designer

The [prefix] convention was never designed — it emerged organically. Agencies are using it to communicate programme context ([KidSTART], [agilePSD-LDS]), not opportunity type. We're asking one field to do two different jobs. Those should be separate.

Engineer

The regex approach has a ceiling. We have 21 unrecognised tag variants today. In 12 months we'll have 50. The right model is a controlled lookup table — a list of approved tags mapped to canonical types — maintained by a product owner, not hardcoded in a script.

"How might we own the tag taxonomy rather than react to whatever agencies create?"
Publish a canonical tag list and communicate it to agencies Quick
A one-page reference doc: approved [prefix] tags, what type they map to, what each type means. Circulate to all agency admins. Doesn't fix existing gigs but prevents new variants from being invented.
Tag lookup table in the ingestion pipeline — admin-editable Medium
Replace the regex with a database table: tag_pattern → canonical_type. A non-engineer can add "[KidSTART] = Secondment" without a code deploy. Unknown tags are surfaced for classification rather than silently TBC'd.
Classify unrecognised tags with a short BO review workflow Medium
New unknown tags are queued for the BO to classify once. Once classified, all gigs with that tag are retroactively updated. Prevents the 109-gig TBC problem from recurring.
Structured Type field in OTG creation form Big bet
The permanent fix. A dropdown with approved types means no free-text prefix parsing needed. Requires OTG product owner buy-in and form change. Could be phased: add the field as optional first, then make mandatory.
Problem area 3 of 5
346 stale gigs will pollute the catalogue if ingested
55% of open gigs have a past end date · 255 have zero applicants
Product Manager

Stale listings destroy applicant trust faster than an empty catalogue. One "Application closed 14 months ago" listing and the user questions everything. We need a clear policy before go-live: do we ingest stale gigs, flag them, or exclude them?

Designer

There are two types of "stale": accidentally stale (agency forgot to close it) and intentionally open-ended (standing roles with no fixed end date). These need different UX treatments. An evergreen posting shouldn't require a fake end date just to pass validation.

Engineer

Staleness is easy to compute — GigEnd < today AND Status = Open. The harder question is what the pipeline does with the result. Exclude entirely: simple. Flag for applicant visibility: requires a OTEP listing-page change. Auto-close: requires a write-back to OTG. Three very different engineering scopes.

"How might we protect the applicant experience from stale listings without penalising agencies that use rolling end dates?"
Hard exclude stale gigs from ingestion (GigEnd < today) Quick
Simplest pipeline rule. Pros: clean catalogue, no stale listings. Cons: excludes legitimate evergreen roles. Mitigate by adding a "Evergreen / No fixed end date" checkbox to the creation form — but that requires a form change.
Auto-exclude stale + zero-applicant gigs only Quick
More permissive: only exclude gigs that are both past their end date AND have never received a single application. 255 gigs would be excluded. Gigs with at least one applicant stay in, on the assumption someone intentionally kept them open.
Surface "Closing soon" / "Recently closed" state on listing card Medium
Ingest stale gigs but show a visual indicator ("Applications may have closed") on the OTEP card. Lets applicants self-select. Requires a listing page UI change. Puts the decision with the applicant, not the pipeline.
Automated stale gig notification to agency admin Medium
30 days before expiry: "Your gig [X] closes in 30 days — extend or close it in OTG." Prevents the backlog from growing. Requires knowing who the admin is (GigOwner) and a reliable email channel.
Problem area 4 of 5
160 gigs may not be enough to launch with
No minimum viable catalogue threshold defined
Product Manager

We've never defined what "enough" looks like. 160 total gigs is already thin. After filtering by agency, type, or function, some views will return single digits. We need to decide: is there a minimum count before we go live, and if so, who unblocks it?

Designer

The problem isn't just count — it's distribution. Even 400 gigs is fine if they're spread across types and functions. But 160 gigs that are 70% Secondments from two agencies means most filter combinations return nothing. We should model what the filtered experience looks like, not just the total.

Engineer

We can model the catalogue at any threshold. If we know which agencies are willing to remediate, we can estimate the realistic passing count post-cleanup. The engineering question is how frequently we can re-run ingestion — if it's daily, agencies can fix and see results quickly.

"How might we define 'good enough to launch' before we pick a go-live date?"
Define minimum viable catalogue: count × distribution Quick
Decision, not engineering. Propose a threshold — e.g. 300 passing gigs, at least 3 opportunity types with 20+ gigs each. Get BO and leadership sign-off before committing to a go-live date.
Target-agency remediation blitz before launch Quick
Enterprise Singapore alone = 178 blocked gigs. A single focused session with their admin team unlocks 38% of all blocked content. Prioritise the top 3 agencies (EnterpriseGov, MTI, MSF) for white-glove remediation support before go-live.
Model catalogue distribution at each remediation milestone Medium
Run a simulation: what does OTEP look like if only EnterpriseGov fixes their gigs? What if MTI also fixes? Build a heat-map of gig coverage by type × function so designers can validate the browse experience at each milestone.
Problem area 5 of 5
Ingestion is a one-time event in our heads, but a recurring operation in practice
Sync cadence, update handling, and ownership undefined
Product Manager

We've been talking about "the ingestion" as if it happens once. But gigs are created, edited, closed, and re-opened continuously. Who runs the ingestion after launch — and how often? If an agency fixes a gig on Tuesday, when does it appear on OTEP? If the answer is "next month", we have a product gap.

Designer

From an applicant's perspective: if I apply for a gig on Monday and it closes on Wednesday, am I notified? If an agency edits the role description after ingestion, does OTEP reflect it? These are continuity-of-experience questions that the current pipeline design doesn't answer.

Engineer

There are three models: (1) full re-ingest on a schedule — simple but slow; (2) delta sync based on DateModified — efficient but requires reliable timestamps; (3) event-driven on OTG save — real-time but requires OTG to emit events. The choice affects how quickly fixes appear on OTEP.

"How might we make OTEP feel live — not like a monthly snapshot?"
Daily scheduled full re-ingest Quick
Run the full pipeline every night. Gigs fixed by an agency appear on OTEP within 24 hours. Simple to operate; no need to track which gigs changed. Acceptable latency for most use cases. Start here.
Delta sync on DateModified — near real-time updates Medium
On each run, only process gigs where DateModified > last_run_timestamp. Reduces processing load. Requires DateModified to be reliably updated in OTG (verify this assumption — some edits may not touch it).
Define and communicate the sync SLA to agencies Quick
Whatever cadence we choose, tell agencies explicitly: "Fixes made before 6pm will appear on OTEP by 9am the next morning." Sets expectations and gives agencies confidence the system is working.

Decisions we need to make this session

These are the blockers. Until they're resolved, the engineering team is building on assumptions.

Decision Owner Deadline Stakes if deferred
What is the minimum viable catalogue for launch? (count + distribution) BO + PM This session No go-live date can be set without it
Is time commitment required for agilePSD and Other (TBC) types? BO This session 109 gigs stuck in amber; remediation report is incomplete
How do we handle stale gigs? (exclude / flag / warn) Trio This session 346 gigs need a disposition; pipeline cannot be finalised without this rule
What is the ingestion cadence? (daily / delta / event-driven) Eng lead This session Determines how quickly agency fixes appear on OTEP; affects agency comms
Who owns the tag taxonomy going forward? PM This session Without an owner, new unclassifiable tags will accumulate after launch
What is the agency feedback mechanism? (email / dashboard / digest) Trio Next sprint Without this, blocked gigs will silently accumulate post-launch
Is there a plan to add a structured Type field in OTG? (timeline + owner) PM Next quarter Without it, type classification remains a regex workaround indefinitely

Proposed session agenda — 90 minutes

0:00 – 0:10
Context alignment discuss Walk through the 5 headline numbers. Agree we're solving the recurring problem, not just the current instance.
0:10 – 0:25
Minimum viable catalogue decide What does OTEP need to look like at launch? Define a threshold. Set the go-live gate.
0:25 – 0:40
Stale gig policy + ingestion cadence decide Choose a staleness rule. Choose a sync cadence. Both are needed before pipeline finalisation.
0:40 – 1:00
Agency feedback loop ideation ideate Pick the highest-value, lowest-effort feedback mechanism for launch. Dot vote on the 4 options in Problem Area 1.
1:00 – 1:15
Tag taxonomy + type classification decide Confirm BO ruling on agilePSD TC rule. Assign taxonomy owner. Agree on lookup table approach vs regex.
1:15 – 1:30
Parking lot + next steps discuss Capture deferred items. Assign actions. Set follow-up cadence (recommend fortnightly trio check-in on OTEP ingestion health).

North star for the quarter

What good looks like
By end of Q3: OTEP launches with a catalogue of at least 350 passing gigs across a minimum of 4 opportunity types. Agency admins receive automated feedback within 24 hours of a gig failing ingestion. The ingestion pipeline runs daily. The tag taxonomy is owned by a named person and documented in a canonical reference. Stale gigs are automatically excluded from the catalogue. The plan to move to a structured Type field in OTG is on the roadmap.
The longer game
The ingestion pipeline is temporary. The permanent solution is a reliable data model in OTG — a Type dropdown, mandatory fields enforced at save, and a real-time event stream to OTEP. Every decision we make in this session should be reversible when that day comes. Build the pipeline in a way that can be deprecated cleanly.

Pre-read for attendees

  • 01_summary_dashboard.html — overall ingestion health; read this first
  • 02_agency_breakdown.html — blocked gigs by agency and type; useful context for the remediation blitz discussion
  • 03_unrecognised_type_analysis.html — the 163 unclassifiable gigs; context for the tag taxonomy decision
  • 04_oqa_risks_assumptions.html — open questions, risks, and assumptions; the full decision log
  • OTEP_Remediation_Report_v2.xlsx — the per-agency remediation report; share with agency admins after the session

The prep doc covers 5 problem areas — each framed through all three lenses, with "how might we" questions, solution ideas tiered by effort (quick win / medium / big bet), and explicit decision prompts.

A few things worth flagging about how the framing diverges from pure data analysis:

The **biggest blind spot the trio would surface** is that the entire current approach treats this as a data cleanup problem when it's actually an ongoing operations problem. The remediation report fixes today's debt; it does nothing about the gig created next Tuesday with the same missing fields. The prep positions that tension explicitly so the session doesn't end with another cleanup exercise.

The **hardest conversation in the room** will be the minimum viable catalogue threshold — because it forces a go/no-go decision that nobody wants to own. Naming it as the first agenda item is intentional: if you don't resolve it early, the session drifts into tactics without a north star.

The **designer's contribution** is probably the most underweighted in what we've built so far. All the work has been pipeline-in, pipeline-out. Nobody has asked what an applicant browsing OTEP with 160 gigs and 12 functions actually experiences. That's the next research thread worth opening.
